Libraries such as Langchain are able to perform language-to-model transformation to generate SQL and perform API calls, thus greatly simplifying the creation of LLM-integrated applications. Not only LLMs come with their own safety problems (Bender et al., 2021; Patel and Pavlick, 2021) but, this convenience arrives also at a cost: in addition to their typical vulnerabilities, LLM-integrated applications are exposed to a new breath of adversarial prompt injection attacks that lead the model to ingest untrusted data, to leak information or to override model safeguards and predefined policies. Typical SQL injection attacks (OWASP, 2023b; Halfond et al., 2006; Marashdeh et al., 2021) have well-known mitigations based on sanitization and source code analysis (Marashdih et al., 2019; Prokhorenko et al., 2016; Damodaran et al., 2017) techniques. LLMs are also susceptible to backdoor attacks where a poisoned dataset can be used to manipulate the LLM into producing a specific answer or exhibiting a specific behavior (Li et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2022) (e.g., producing a DROP TABLE statement). Recently, a new attack vector known as indirect prompt injections, was identified (Greshake et al., 2023) in which the LLM is led to ingest prompt instructions retrieved from API call (e.g., the results of a SQL query). Overall, the attacks mentioned can compromise the integrity and security of the LLM’s responses, potentially leading to undesired actions or leaking sensitive information; yet, despite their effects, adequate approaches for their mitigation are still an open topic. In this scenario, the user of the LLM system is an innocent bystander who is often the victim of the attack. The malicious actor places instructive text in the external source. Since LLMs are “eager” to adhere to any detected instructions, the model may take the malicious instructions as desired intent from the user and then act upon those instructions. The nascent threat of XPIA has been studied and demonstrated by security researchers. As LLM systems become equipped with more plugins or access patterns, the downstream risks of XPIA become ele

We refer to these as user prompt injection attacks (UPIA) and their intent is characterized by a user (malicious or curious) who directly attempts to subvert the model’s safety rules. The semantic variety of these attacks is vast, ranging from clever naturalistic attacks to uninterpretable (but effective) token-based attacks [21]. While many of the semantics and tactics of UPIA could transfer over to XPIA, the XPIA problem yields a different distribution of language use. That is, a typical XPIA might entail a lengthy document with a small (or even perceptually invisible) attack pattern within. The XPIA problem can seen a superset of the UPIA problem. For example, the rather benign instruction of “Please transfer fifty dollars to account number 54321” could be a non-harmful prompt in a user-driven setting, but a malicious attack in an XPIA setting. While securing general-purpose agents remains out of reach with current capabilities, we argue that application-specific agents can be secured through principled system design. To support this claim, we propose six design patterns for making AI agents resilient to prompt injection attacks. These patterns are intentionally simple, making them easier to analyze and reason about — an essential property for deploying AI in high-stakes or safety-critical settings. We demonstrate the practical applicability of these patterns through ten case studies spanning diverse domains.

First, forgetting: fast-rate adaptation to evolving patterns progressively overwrites prior detection knowledge, degrading recognition of earlier attack variants and risking misidentification of familiar normal behaviors as anomalous [14]. Second, robustness: precisely disentangling adversarially-induced drift from legitimate behavioral drift in real time is non-trivial, as conflating the two sources leads to either missed attacks or excessive false alarms [15]. Third, generalization: adversaries continuously introduce novel attack strategies outside the training distribution, which existing detectors tend to misclassify as normal, leaving the system exposed in open-world deployments [16, 17]. To address these challenges, we propose OpenEvoShield (Figure 1(c)), a co-evolutionary continual defense framework for LLM-MAS comprising four synergistic modules. Motivated by the weak-to-strong signal escalation paradigm [18], the Asymmetric Co-Evolutionary Rate Controller (M1) serves as the o

The challenge is to make properties such as context ownership and capability attestation verifiable protocol invariants, analyzing the A2A↔\leftrightarrowMCP boundary as a single security surface rather than optional implementer guidance. Agent identity and delegated authorization. Agentic systems lack a coherent model of who is acting and with what authority. Within a single agent, broad tool permissions allow individually authorized actions to compose into unintended effects, creating confused-deputy scenarios that per

nance. Relayed credentials without sender constraints or reuse restrictions further allow a compromised intermediary to replay credentials across the delegation chain (Cisco, 2025). Existing standards provide building blocks for addressing these gaps. OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) supports signed delegation chains, while audience restriction (RFC 8707) and sender-constrained tokens (DPoP, RFC 9449) enable least-privilege delegation and limit credential reuse. The challenge is not the absence of these mechanisms, but that current agent interoperability protocols treat them as optional, preventing interoperating agents from assuming that delegated identities are securely propagated, constrained, and replay-resistant. Emergent multi-agent risk. A compromise need not stay local to one agent. Prompt Infection shows a malicious instruction can self-replicate from agent to agent like a virus, propagating silently through a multi-agent system even when agents do not share all communication (Lee et

need not stay local to one agent. Prompt Infection shows a malicious instruction can self-replicate from agent to agent like a virus, propagating silently through a multi-agent system even when agents do not share all communication (Lee et al., 2026). Zero-click GenAI worms generalize this to self-propagating payloads that spread through the applications agents are embedded in (Cohen et al., 2024). Model Routing: The Control Plane Beneath The attack surfaces discussed so far concern the execution and collaboration layers of the agentic ecosystem. Production systems introduce a third: the model-routing control plan

ent, and cost profile handle the request. This creates a third attack surface, the agent-to-model control plane, underlying both agent-to-tool and agent-to-agent interactions. Adversarial Routing. The routing decision can be attacked across the stack. At the input level, crafted token sequences can force cost-inflating model upgrades (Shafran et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026) or downgrade requests to cheaper, less-aligned models, creating a jailbreak-by-downgrade that bypasses per-tool privilege checks (Shafran et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026). Router architecture is itself a security variable. Trainable neural routers are more susceptible to adversarial suffixes and training-time backdoors than parameter-free similarity routers, making robustness an architectural choice (Lin et al., 2025). The attack surface also extends into model internals. In mixture-of-experts models, adversarial inputs can suppress safety-critical experts, leak prompts through cross-batch routing dependenc

r trigger denial-of-service through expert imbalance (Xu et al., 2026; Yona et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). These failures occur inside the routing topology and may remain invisible at the output level. Current defenses primarily focus on detection. Contrastive detectors can identify rerouting prompts before execution with strong reported accuracy (Zhang et al., 2026), but they provide no certified robustness, lack evaluation against adaptive attackers, and do not address in-model or cross-batch attacks. The challenge is to treat routing as a policy artifact. A recent declarative approach compiles routing logic into a non-Turing-complete specification with exhaustive, conflict-free decisions, audit trails, and verified routing nodes across MCP and A2A boundaries (Chen et al., 2026), reflecting the broader shift from advisory guidance to enforceable invariants. Routing Provenance and Observability. The router is itself a supply-chain component. Its weights, training data, and decision thresholds

Existing safety mechanisms are not designed to address this class of failures. Runtime guards enforce stateless, per-action policies (Wang et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026) without reasoning about how system state evolves over an long execution trajectory. LLM-to-formal-spec compilers derive rules from specifications (Zhou et al., 2026; Miculicich et al., 2025) but cannot guarantee completeness, consistency, or faithfulness to the governing standards. Probabilistic monitors learn from observed execution traces (Wang et al., 2025a). A recent line of work enforces hand-authored temporal, state-dependent properties at runtime (Kamath et al., 2025). As a result, content added to memory during one session may reappear later without the agent suspecting it [1, 2]. This is partly because retrieval compares similarity rather than verifying trustworthiness. So a convincingly fabricated memory can rank as high as a legitimate one [3, 4]. Recent research further elaborates on the attack surface, highlighting activities at writing, retrieval, and action stage

uation pattern in this work is consistent: construct an attack, test if the defense prevents it, and report the decline in attack success rate [9, 14]. This overlooks what the defense does when no attack occurs, which is most of the time in deployment. The systems literature complements this by focusing on benchmarking memory architectures on accuracy, latency, and token cost [16, 17], often without any defense layered on top [18, 19]. What a defense costs when there is no attack to catch lies between these two literatures, and this paper measures that cost. ## 3 Threat Model and Defenses ## 3.1 Pipeline The agent we analyze follows the typical structure of memory-augmented systems. Conversations unfold one turn at a time. At each turn, an extraction step decides what, if anything, to remember and stores it in a vector store. For each question, the most similar memories are retrieved and added to the model’s context. A defense can intervene at three points. Write screens content before storage.

w.t: nd adapt ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) . For RSI, the critical question is whether a safety failure remains local or becomes embedded in the processes shaping future system versions. Existing research approaches these challenges from complementary directions. Surveys of RSI and self-evolving agents examine the mechanisms and development of self-improving systems ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026a ; Ren et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . Agent-security surveys investigate threats such as prompt injection, data poisoning, and privacy leakage ( Deng et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ; Ling et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , while foundational studies of self-modification examine the preservation of objectives as agents modify themselves ( Schmidhuber, 2007 ; Orseau and Ring, 2011 ; Everitt et al., 2016 ) . Together, these studies provide important foundations, but a broader question remains insufficiently addressed, i.e., how safety-relevant changes are introduced and selected during self-improvement, r

ety , a perspective on how safety properties are preserved, weakened, or restored across successive rounds of self-improvement. The concern extends beyond whether an individual update is safe to how its effects persist and influence subsequent changes. Current systems already provide mechanisms for such dependencies: agents retain and reuse experience through memories, skills, and tools ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2025 ) ; self-rewarding methods incorporate generated evaluations into improvement ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) ; and automated development systems extend improvement to agent designs and research workflows ( Hu et al., 2025a ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ) . Although these systems differ in the scope of self-improvement they support, they illustrate how earlier changes can shape future system behavior. For example, a coding agent may retain a permission-bypassing repair as a reusable skill, allowing the unsafe behavio

repair as a reusable skill, allowing the unsafe behavior to persist even after the original input is removed. Assessing such risks therefore requires tracing safety-relevant changes across subsequent updates and the systems that inherit their effects. Our study is guided by four questions: what makes safety evolutionary, how safety degrades as systems improve, which domains carry or mediate safety-relevant changes, and how the resulting risks can be discovered and assessed (Figure 3 ). We examine how persistence, mutable scope, and loop closure shape the transition from local improvement to recursive development, and characterize six recurring manifestations of evolutionary risk. To understand where these risks arise and how they evolve, we develop a five-domain taxonomy and an evaluation framework spanning states, accepted updates, trajectories, and lineages. We further discuss governance principles for modification boundaries, independent verification and authorization, provenance, and recovery.

al improvement revises behavior within an episode without retaining the change; persistent system adaptation carries updates into later interactions; and recursive development modifies the procedures used to generate, evaluate, or admit future updates. Many current systems support persistent adaptation without necessarily modifying their update procedures, while already involving selection and inheritance mechanisms relevant to RSI safety ( Ren et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . Continual-learning research provides related concepts, including the stability–plasticity trade-off and catastrophic forgetting, although capability forgetting does not necessarily imply safety degradation ( Parisi et al., 2019 ) . A Self-Improving Coding Agent illustrates persistent modification by revising its orchestration code and reporting benchmark improvements ( Robeyns et al., 2025 ) . Whether such changes constitute recursive development depends on their effects on subsequent update procedure

Research Agenda Treating memory as middleware opens a research agenda the systems community is well positioned to take on. The agenda has a dependency structure. Two items are foundational: the programming model and common interface of Section 3 (what an agent declares, queries, and governs) and consistency semantics for learned experience, because every other mechanism is specified against them. Admission, forgetting/eviction, deployment-aware packaging, and purpose-directed compression build on those foundations. Isolation and sharing policies, provenance, and portability benchmarks are cross-cutting and can proceed in parallel. We therefore develop the two foundational items in the most depth below. Foundational: Consistency models for learned experience. Traditional storage consistency does not transfer, because memories are generated interpretations of experience rather than ground-truth records. Future

ing candidate memories, checking for conflicts, updating existing memories, and publishing selected items—which require transactional semantics and failure handling; middleware should define atomicity, rollback, and approval policies for memory writes. The natural transaction unit is the staged write pipeline of Section 4 —capture, extract, consolidate, publish—with defined rollback points: a failed consolidation must not leave half-merged guidance retrievable, and an unapproved candidate must not influence behavior while it awaits review. Building on the foundations: Memory admission and quality-weighted learning. Not every experience deserves to become memory: an agent that learns indiscriminately internalizes the mistakes of failed runs as readily as the insights of successful ones. Middleware therefore needs an admission stage that scores a candidate experience before distilling it and weights the result by source quality, combining heterogeneous, partly reliable signals—task outcomes, agent se

Write-path, admission, and retrieval policy. Recent systems ask what to store and when : embedding-based write admission ( Hu et al., 2026 ) , recurrence-triggered consolidation ( Dai et al., 2026 ) , causal rather than similarity-based selection ( Srivastava, 2026 ) , closed-loop tuning of memory operations ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , and empirical studies of memory management ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) . These motivate our write-path-consistency and admission agenda, framed as policies a memory layer should own rather than each agent. Trust, provenance, and portability. Persistent memory introduces new attack surfaces and governance needs: memory poisoning ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , lineage and post-hoc audit ( Ouyang and Hou, 2026 ; Tan et al., 2026 ) , governed evolving memory ( Lam et al., 2026 ) , se

Skills as procedural memory. Procedural memory increasingly materializes as reusable skills discovered, refined, and curated from experience ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) , though skills can also add overhead or harm ( Chacko et al., 2026 ) ; our procedural memory and consolidation are complementary, and governed skill promotion is part of our agenda. Memory services and platforms. Productized memory layers ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) , managed platform memories ( Anthropic, 2026 ; GitHub, 2025 ; Amazon Web Services, 2025 ; Google Cloud, 2026 ; Cloudflare, 2026 ; Oracle, 2026 ) , framework primitives ( LangChain, 2025 ) , and file-native memories ( AGENTS.md contributors, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026a ; OpenClaw, 2026 ) are strong on storage and governance but are typically bound to one host or cloud, with semantics centered on personalization and session continuity. We instead offer a host- and store-portable substrate with the cross-cutting guarantees—two-sided pluggability, isolation, consistency, sharing, and lifecycle governance—none of these expose uniformly. 8. Conclusion Agents are becoming persistent software actors, but their me

ersistent software actors, but their memory remains fragmented application logic. We have argued that it should instead be a first-class middleware substrate—one that interposes between agents and stores, learns from experience, and governs the result. altk-evolve ( AgentToolkit, 2026 ) shows that an initial subset is practical and improves agent reliability; the broader challenge—defining the abstractions, consistency models, policies, and benchmarks that make memory a reusable foundation for self-improving agents—is now open to the systems community. To understand how residual authority arises in practice, we recover and validate the native authorization semantics of eight production coding agents, detailed in Appendix C. Table 1 summarizes how these systems store approval state, how precisely they match later actions, and how long that state remains effective. We find that authorization state from prior interactions can persist across task and session boundaries, allowing subsequent actions to bypass otherwise-required user approval, as demonstrated for Codex in Appendix E. These observations expose a temporal blind spot in least privilege. A grant of authority may be minimal when issued but become excessive once it outlives the context that justified it (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975). The failure echoes the structure of a time-of-check to time-of-use flaw, where a security decision made under one state remains operative after the relevant state has changed (Bishop e

Conleash develops reusable consent rules to reduce repeated approval friction (Li et al., 2026). Authorization Continuity studies when earned authority should remain valid as an agent or its context evolves (Zhang and Zhang, 2026), while Lingering Authority addresses stale reuse by revoking temporary capabilities once their justifying episode ends (Santos-Grueiro, 2026a). Related work further studies authorization closure and stale security state (Santos-Grueiro, 2026b; Wu et al., 2026). These works primarily constrain the validity of existing authority. w.t: roduction Memory is fundamental for language agents operating over extended interactions. Without persistent memory, agents cannot reliably retain user-specific information, connect events across sessions, or reuse past experience in future decisions. Prior work has therefore developed mechanisms for storing, retrieving, and managing information beyond the immediate context window, ranging from memory streams and memory banks to more structured and adaptive memory systems [10, 18, 9, 1, 15, 6]. Despite this progress, most systems still form memories by directly extracting or compressing conversational context. This can overlook useful evidence, while details discarded at formation time may later become important for unforeseen queries. Relying only on compressed memory prevents such information from being recovered, whereas full-history fallback incurs substantial inference cost [17]. These limitations motivate selective access to source dialogue during both memory formation and memory use. To t

RIME achieves the strongest performance across LLM-Judge, F1, and BLEU-1 among the compared methods while requiring substantially fewer query-time LLM tokens than deliberative memory baselines. ## 2 Related Work Long-term memory for language agents. Long-term memory systems have evolved from persistent external memory stores [10, 18, 9] toward more sophisticated mechanisms for constructing and maintaining compact memory. Mem0 [1] consolidates extracted facts through explicit memory operations, while A-MEM [15] organizes memories as dynamically linked and evolving notes. Nemori [6] and FadeMem [14] focus on selective retention, through semantic distillation and adaptive forgetting, respectively. SimpleMem [5] and LightMem [2] improve efficiency through structured compression, consolidation, and hierarchical memory management. Despite their different designs, these methods mainly optimize how observed interaction content is transformed, organized, or maintained as memory. RIME intervenes one step

ettings; A-MEM retains its original all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding model following its official configuration. The source code, including the exact prompts and evaluation configuration, is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RIME_official-4BC7. ## 4.2 Main Results Table 1 compares RIME with representative long-term memory systems under two LLM backbones. RIME consistently achieves the best performance across all three quality metrics with both Qwen3-235B-A22B and GPT-5.6 Sol. Notably, these gains are achieved with substantially lower query-time LLM cost than deliberative memory baselines such as A-MEM and Nemori, demonstrating that selective access to source dialogue provides an effective alternative to expensive deliberation over long histories. We further examine whether access to the source dialogue is necessary when semantic memory is insufficient. [TABLE] ## 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate as persistent software systems that browse, write files, call tools, and maintain user-specific state. Because fixed prompts and workflows cannot anticipate every deployment condition, self-evolution offers a natural mechanism for continual adaptation. Parameter-free harness updates have become a popular design choice (31, 32, 23), especially for agents that run API-based frontier models with black-box access. These updates act on the agent’s memory, controller policies, and reusable skills from interaction history and feedback, improving capability without changing model weights. But this capability also creates a new safety issue (22). Unlike for static agents, loca

ecent literature for stateful and tool-augmented, but non-evolving, agents and their susceptibility to indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, manipulation through retrieved content, and long-horizon adversarial prompting (9, 5, 6, 28, 33, 13, 4). Additionally, prior works show that even ostensibly benign parameter-based optimization can erode safety for aligned models, narrow optimization can induce broader misalignment, and utility-improving interventions can unintentionally increase downstream risk (18, 2, 7, 27, 11). Therefore, an interesting open area of safety investigation concerns agents that perform parameter-free self-updates. Contributions. To address these gaps, we introduce SEABench and make four contributions: (1) a benchmark for jointly studying capability growth and endogenous misalignment across longitudinal personal-assistant tasks, without direct adversarial intervention or agent modification, spanning multiple task domains and harm types on a rich personal assistant enviro

ten within a single domain or task family. A number of approaches center self-evolution at the level of model parameters (21, 10); while effective, such updates alter the model’s internal representation space and may introduce unintended side effects. Prior work has shown that optimization for utility can unexpectedly degrade safety: benign fine-tuning can weaken safety alignment (18), benign adaptation for helpfulness can break contextual privacy (7), activation steering for seemingly orthogonal utility goals can increase jailbreak risk (27), and fine-tuning on safeguarded outputs can elicit harmful capabilities (11). Therefore, a more non-trivial safety investigation can involve parameter-update-free self-evolution at the agent level, where agents reflect on experience and revise persistent external state such as controller files, memory, and reusable skills or tools (31, 32), through which local interactions may become durable behavioral changes. Continual-learning and self-evolving agentic systems involve persistent updates to components such as memory, skills, workflows, safety mechanisms, and attack–defense strategies, which can in turn affect subsequent behavior, candidate generation, and evaluation [ 30 , 31 ] . Co-evolution provides a natural way to model this reciprocal adaptation. We construct a compositional attack benchmark from 4,000 public skills across eight cybersecurity behaviors, providing a systematic testbed for evaluating composition-induced risks and stress-testing future skill vetting mechanisms. ## 2 Related Works ## 2.1 Security of Agent Skills LLM agents increasingly rely on skills to extend their functionality with task-specific instructions, executable procedures, and access to external resources. As public repositories make these skills easier to discover, install, and reuse, agents can rapidly incorporate capabilities contributed by different developers. This convenience also introduces security concerns, since a downloaded skill may contain unsafe instructions, suspicious executable logic, excessive res

e, as agents increasingly use multiple skills within the same task, security risks may also arise from how otherwise benign functions are combined during execution, extending the security problem beyond what can be observed from each skill separately. ## 2.2 Security in Agent Skill Ecosystems To support complex tasks that require different forms of knowledge, procedures, and tool use, LLM agents may employ multiple skills within the same workflow. As these skills are selected and combined according to task requirements, they collectively form an agent skill ecosystem in which independently developed capabilities can participate in a shared execution. Recent work has explored different coordination mechanisms: AgentSkillOS organizes skills through structured execution pipelines (Li et al., 2026), SkillWeaver decomposes requests and composes retrieved skills into executable plans (Gao, 2026), SkillComposer jointly selects skills and their execution order (Zhao et al., 2026), and R3-Skill considers

three standalone skill vetting engines: SkillSafe (SkillSafe, 2026), Cisco Skill Scanner (Cisco AI Defense, 2026), and Tencent Cloud Security Center SkillScan (CSC SkillScan) (Tencent Cloud, 2026). SkillSafe serves as the vetting constraint during RRS. For unsuccessful original compositions, RRS performs up to T=5T=5 optimization rounds with five candidate compositions generated at each round. Optimization terminates once SRC confirms the target environmental consequence or the iteration budget is exhausted. We report Attack Success Rate (ASR). An attack succeeds when SRC confirms the target environmental consequence. ## 6.2 Attack Effectiveness across Models and Optimization Settings We evaluate CRIME under DCA and three ACA configurations that refine Skill A, Skill B, or both skills, using the same skill pairs and execution settings across DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-4o-mini. More recently, several studies have explored structural, semantic, and runtime auditing mechanisms for detecting untrusted or malicious skills before or during deployment (Lv et al., 2026; Etteib et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). The correct solution is conditional enrichment governed by scope classification at formation time. ## 3 Gated Memory Gated Memory is a drop-in formation layer that sits between conversation and any existing memory backend, decomposing into three sequential stages: admission, scope classification, and conditional enrichment (Figure 1). A naive formation layer that consumes the entire visible dialogue history on every turn re-evaluates, and therefore re-emits, facts it has already committed: the same attribute is written on every subsequent turn in which it remains visible, and unbound references in the history are resolved against the wrong antecedent, fabricating entities that the current turn never mention

an internal lesson store for anomalous paths. For each query, the retrieved or retained experience set is treated as the validation input, and the defense constructs a reasoning path from each record before estimating its divergence from the consensus. A record is treated as anomalous when it is explicitly judged anomalous or when its divergence score exceeds 0.50.5; such records are quarantined and converted into negative lessons. Relevant lessons are then retrieved from the internal store and supplied alongside the learned policy memory for downstream decision making. When consensus validation is undefined, such as for a single-record input, the defense explicitly bypasses validation rather than treating the record as safe. A prompt injection in any of that content can direct the agent to read credentials, modify files that later run with more privilege, or send data away [28, 17, 69]. Model-level defenses such as structured queries [8], instruction hierarchies [57], and input marking [30] reduce attack success, but adaptive attackers continue to bypass them [68, 38]. The exploits disclosed against them in 2025 and 2026 show where these mechanisms fail. A read-only command allowlist admitted options that run code or write files [46]; in one case an allowlisted git show wrote a crafted format string over .git/config with --output, and the next routine git diff ran the external diff driver it defined [22]. Six assistants wrote through a project file that was a symlink to a file in the user’s home directory, and their approval dialogs showed the name of the link [20]. At the summary layer, where one flat receipt has to vouch for several sentences, they are wrong about two thirds of the time, almost always by keeping content that no longer re-derives. On Bemula, we evaluate six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs, together with the Full Context LLM on two of them. The results are negative. During each task run, the driver records command events, completion status, and generated artifacts, while a local proxy records network requests. HITL’s risk rules (Shan et al., 2026) are extracted from its tool-call classification and extended rule layers and applied to serialized tool names and arguments. They check both individual calls and their order in the execution trace, counting a HIGH or CRITICAL match as a detection. DefenseClaw’s strict-policy rules (Cisco AI Defense, 2026a), rated HIGH or CRITICAL, are applied to tool commands, proxy-recorded network requests, and installed Python, shell, JSON,

l model signals (Xiao et al., 2026), declared–implemented capability comparisons (Wu et al., 2026), and repository context (Holzbauer et al., 2026). ChainGuard extends auditing to dependencies between candidate and installed skills (Zeng et al., 2026). At runtime, AgentSpec and Progent constrain actions and privileges (Wang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2025), HITL and DefenseClaw assess risks and apply policies (Shan et al., 2026; Cisco AI Defense, 2026a), and SkillDetonate audits sandbox behavior through information-flow evidence (Ji et al., 2026). Execution-based evaluation complements these defenses. ToolEmu emulates tool execution (Ruan et al., 2024), InjecAgent tests indirect injection (Zhan et al., 2024), and AgentDojo evaluates legitimate tasks alongside adversarial objectives (Debenedetti et al., 2024). ASB studies attacks across agent components and the utility–security balance (Zhang et al., 2025), while MalSkillBench verifies malicious skills through sandbox execution (Guo et al., 2026a).

Depending on the task, agents may pursue individual or shared objectives, cooperate or compete, and divide tasks according to their roles. They may also be organized through centralized, hierarchical, or decentralized architectures. A typical MAS comprises: agents, environments, interactions, and communication [11]. Accordingly, a system’s security depends not only on the properties of its individual agents but also on their coordination and information exchange, particularly where these processes cross trust boundaries [2].

This poses new challenges for identity management, as traditional identity access management (IAM) was not designed for such environments. We must therefore accurately limit the scope of what an AI agent’s identity is. In general, it is understood as a composition of different attributes, describing its capabilities, behavior, relationships, attestations, origin, and purpose [7]. This set depends on implementation. KEMTLS redesigns the TLS handshake by replacing the online handshake using heavy PQC signatures [21] with implicit authentication based on key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs) especially ML-KEM, for key exchange and authentication. In this flow, the responding agent’s certificate would contain KEM public key rather than signature verification key, only the holder of the corresponding private key can decapsulate the shared secret and derive the session key. These capabilities have also been largely used for robotic task planning and decision-making (Li et al., 2026; Driess et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023b). As LLMs are increasingly used to translate natural-language instructions into robot behavior (Ahn et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023a; Rana et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023), their vulnerabilities can le

autonomously designing and executing scientific research (Boiko et al., 2023; Wuwu et al., 2025). These capabilities have also been largely used for robotic task planning and decision-making (Li et al., 2026; Driess et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023b). As LLMs are increasingly used to translate natural-language instructions into robot behavior (Ahn et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023a; Rana et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023), their vulnerabilities can lead to physical safety risks. BadRobot (Zhang et al., 2025) and RoboPAIR (Robey et al., 2025) show that jailbreak attacks can induce harmful actions in LLM-controlled robots. Unlike a chatbot’s harmful text, these are actions executed in the world and can be difficult to reverse. In response, inference-time defenses aim to verify robot behavior before execution. RoboGuard (Ravichandran et al., 2026) grounds safety rules into world-specific Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) constraints for formal verification, while SafePlan (Obi et al., 20

tructions that target one hazardous behavior, and they often concentrate safety verification in a single stage. Such single-stage verification becomes unreliable when a hazardous step is hidden among many legitimate steps of a long-horizon instruction. The reason could be that LLMs become less reliable as a task grows longer and more complex, especially when they must reason about the whole task at once (Liu et al., 2024; Besta et al., 2024). Moreover, some existing defenses rely on formal safety specifications written in LTL. When such a specification is produced by an LLM in a single unverified pass, it may not reflect the scene properly, and our experiments show that on long-horizon compound tasks the resulting constraints can be incomplete or incorrect. As a result, a defense that judges the instruction as a whole may either overlook the hidden unsafe sub-task or reject the instruction and discard its legitimate parts. As a result, a defense that judges the instruction as a whole may either overlook the hidden unsafe sub-task or reject the instruction and discard its legitimate parts. For example, in Figure 1 (right), RoboGuard accepts the hazardous sub-task of leaving the oven on with its door open, whereas SafePlan refuses the instruction altogether, including the harmless request to put the oven mitt on the counter. We therefore argue that, instead of simply accepting or rejecting an instruction, an LLM-enabled robot should refuse its harmful sub-tasks while completing its legitimate ones, a problem we refer to as safe task completion. The larger rollout group used by GRPO is restricted to the GRPO baseline and is not used by RSD. ## Teacher and Privileged-Context Configuration. The teacher retrospectively re-scores the student’s on-policy trajectories under privileged context and provides the next-token distributions used for distillation. w.t: . When stored content returns to the context through a retrieval or a checkpoint restore, it already has a descriptor, but that descriptor may no longer be valid. Reload therefore compares the counters recorded in the descriptor with the current ones. Suppose the owner reports the invoice as forged and revokes it, so its counter goes from 0 to 1. When the agent later retrieves the summary, reload sees that the summary recorded the invoice at 0 and does not trust the stored descriptor. The summary instead goes through map again. Because the current counters are kept outside checkpoints, restoring an old checkpoint cannot make the summary valid again. This check therefore stops use-after-revoke, the use of memory whose source has been revoked. ## Acting (authorize). The model’s decision to call a tool may be influenced by anything in its context. Controlling that decision would require ClawMMU to understand what the content means and how the model reasons about it, which no label captures. Authori

ed Work and Guarantees The inheritance rule of ClawMMU, which gives derived memory the lowest authority of its inputs, is the classical low-water-mark integrity policy, in which anything that reads untrusted data becomes untrusted itself (Biba, 1977). Compartments and the rule that only the owner raises authority follow operating systems such as HiStar (Zeldovich et al., 2006) and Flume (Krohn et al., 2007), which label every object and control data flow between labels. Agent memory adds two cases these systems did not face, because an untrusted model produces derived data and checkpoints restore old state. Recent agent defenses each cover part of this problem, but none combines memory labels, revocation that survives checkpoint restore, and per-argument checks (Debenedetti et al., 2026; Louck, 2026; Ouyang and Hou, 2026; Li et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). Appendix C compares their guarantees system by system. ClawMMU also adds owner-and-scope separation that is denied by default. ## 5 Vision

On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley–Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indisp

Where skills help turns out to depend sharply on how the problem was synthesized (Figure 8(a)). On structure synthesis problems, which reuse a few recurring patterns, recursively evolved skills cut the agent’s tool use: as the library grows, tool calls drop by 44% (from 3232 to 1818 per question) while MAPE stays at least as strong as the skill-free baseline. One encounter is often enough for Athena to distil a skill that captures the whole family, letting Branchus skip exploratory search and act on a compiled shortcut. The parameter axis benefits in the same direction. Relative to plain RFT, RFT on the adversarially synthesized hard problems improves every forecasting metric we track, lowering the Brier score by 1.6%1.6\%, raising AUROC by 2.7%2.7\%, and tightening numeric forecasts by 1.0%1.0\% in relative WIS and 4.0%4.0\% in Md-sAPE (Figure 10). Because both axes draw on the same enriched experience, the evolved environment lifts the system through the skills it distils and the parameters it updates alike. The agent and its environment thus enter a productive cycle: each round of environment evolution exposes a weakness, and each round of agent evolution repairs it, so capability compounds rather than saturates. B Experiments on the AgentDojo Benchmark AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) is a benchmark designed to evaluate IPI attacks on LLM agents within a dynamic simulated environment. It encompasses four distinct scenarios: workspace, Slack, travel, and banking. From each scenario, we selected two attacker cases and two user cases, forming a test set of 16 cases in total, which we then evaluated on the Llama3-8B based agent. Table

Although adaptive attacks still yield substantial improvements in ASR, they are not as effective as on the InjecAgent benchmark—where all adaptive attack ASRs exceed 50%. We hypothesize that this discrepancy arises primarily from the significantly longer contexts in AgentDojo, with an average token length of 3,823 and a maximum of 6,152, compared to InjecAgent’s average token length of 1,033 and maximum of 1,711. These longer contexts, which often include multiple rounds of agent-tool interaction, pose greater challenges for optimizing the adversarial string.
